verses.text: He who resolves to love God, and to love his neighbor as himself, not according to man but according to God, is on account of this love said to be of a good will; and this is in Scripture more commonly called charity, but it is also, even in the same books, called love.
verses.modernizedText: He who resolves to love God, and to love his neighbor as himself, not according to man but according to God, is on account of this love said to be of a good will; and this is in Scripture more commonly called charity, but it is also, even in the same books, called love.

verses.text: For the apostle says that the man to be elected as a ruler of the people must be a lover of good.
verses.modernizedText: For the apostle says that the man to be elected as a ruler of the people must be a lover of good.

verses.text: And when the Lord Himself had asked Peter, “Hast thou a regard for me (diligis) more than these?”
verses.modernizedText: And when the Lord Himself had asked Peter, “Have you a regard for me (diligis) more than these?”

verses.text: Peter replied, “Lord, Thou knowest that I love (amo) Thee.”
verses.modernizedText: Peter replied, “Lord, You know that I love (amo) You.”

verses.text: And again a second time the Lord asked not whether Peter loved (amaret) Him, but whether he had a regard (diligeret)for Him, and, he again answered, “Lord, Thou knowest that I love (amo) Thee.”
verses.modernizedText: And again a second time the Lord asked not whether Peter loved (amaret) Him, but whether he had a regard (diligeret)for Him, and, he again answered, “Lord, You know that I love (amo) You.”

verses.text: But on the third interrogation the Lord Himself no longer says, “Hast thou a regard (diligis) for me,”but “Lovest thou (amas) me?”
verses.modernizedText: But on the third interrogation the Lord Himself no longer says, “Have you a regard (diligis) for me,”but “Love you (amas) me?”

verses.text: And then the evangelist adds, “Peter was grieved because He said unto him the third time, “Lovest thou (amas) me?” though the Lord had not said three times but only once, “Lovest thou (amas) me?” and twice “Diligis me ?” from which we gather that, even when the Lord said “diligis,” He used an equivalent for “amas.”
verses.modernizedText: And then the evangelist adds, “Peter was grieved because He said to him the third time, “Love you (amas) me?” though the Lord had not said three times but only once, “Love you (amas) me?” and twice “Diligis me ?” from which we gather that, even when the Lord said “diligis,” He used an equivalent for “amas.”

verses.text: Peter, too, throughout used one word for the one thing, and the third time also replied, “Lord, Thou knowest all things, Thou knowest that I love (amo) Thee.”
verses.modernizedText: Peter, too, throughout used one word for the one thing, and the third time also replied, “Lord, You know all things, You know that I love (amo) You.”

verses.text: I have judged it right to mention this, because some are of opinion that charity or regard (dilectio) is one thing, love (amor) another.
verses.modernizedText: I have judged it right to mention this, because some are of opinion that charity or regard (dilectio) is one thing, love (amor) another.

verses.text: They say that dilectio is used of a good affection, amor of an evil love.
verses.modernizedText: They say that dilectio is used of a good affection, amor of an evil love.

verses.text: But it is very certain that even secular literature knows no such distinction.
verses.modernizedText: But it is very certain that even secular literature knows no such distinction.

verses.text: However, it is for the philosophers to determine whether and how they differ, though their own writings sufficiently testify that they make great account of love (amor) placed on good objects, and even on God Himself.
verses.modernizedText: However, it is for the philosophers to determine whether and how they differ, though their own writings sufficiently testify that they make great account of love (amor) placed on good objects, and even on God Himself.

verses.text: But we wished to show that the Scriptures of our religion, whose authority we prefer to all writings whatsoever, make no distinction between amor, dilectio, and caritas; and we have already shown that amor is used in a good connection.
verses.modernizedText: But we wished to show that the Scriptures of our religion, whose authority we prefer to all writings whatsoever, make no distinction between amor, dilectio, and caritas; and we have already shown that amor is used in a good connection.

verses.text: And if any one fancy that amor is no doubt used both of good and bad loves, but that dilectio is reserved for the good only, let him remember what the psalm says, “He that loveth (diligit) iniquity hateth his own soul;” and the words of the Apostle John, “If any man love (diligere) the world, the love (dilectio) of the Father is not in him.”
verses.modernizedText: And if any one fancy that amor is no doubt used both of good and bad loves, but that dilectio is reserved for the good only, let him remember what the psalm says, “He that loves (diligit) iniquity hates his own soul;” and the words of the Apostle John, “If any man love (diligere) the world, the love (dilectio) of the Father is not in him.”

verses.text: Here you have in one passage dilectio used both in a good and a bad sense.
verses.modernizedText: Here you have in one passage dilectio used both in a good and a bad sense.

verses.text: And if any one demands an instance of amor being used in a bad sense (for we have already shown its use in a good sense), let him read the words, “For men shall be lovers (amantes) of their own selves, lovers (amatores) of money.”
verses.modernizedText: And if any one demands an instance of amor being used in a bad sense (for we have already shown its use in a good sense), let him read the words, “For men shall be lovers (amantes) of their own selves, lovers (amatores) of money.”

verses.text: The right will is, therefore, well-directed love, and the wrong will is ill-directed love.
verses.modernizedText: The right will is, therefore, well-directed love, and the wrong will is ill-directed love.

verses.text: Love, then, yearning to have what is loved, is desire; and having and enjoying it, is joy; fleeing what is opposed to it, it is fear; and feeling what is opposed to it, when it has befallen it, it is sadness.
verses.modernizedText: Love, then, yearning to have what is loved, is desire; and having and enjoying it, is joy; fleeing what is opposed to it, it is fear; and feeling what is opposed to it, when it has befallen it, it is sadness.

verses.text: Now these motions are evil if the love is evil; good if the love is good.
verses.modernizedText: Now these motions are evil if the love is evil; good if the love is good.

verses.text: What we assert let us prove from Scripture.
verses.modernizedText: What we assert let us prove from Scripture.

verses.text: The apostle “desires to depart, and to be with Christ.”
verses.modernizedText: The apostle “desires to depart, and to be with Christ.”

verses.text: And, “My soul desired to long for Thy judgments;” or if it is more appropriate to say, “My soul longed to desire Thy judgments.”
verses.modernizedText: And, “My soul desired to long for Your judgments;” or if it is more appropriate to say, “My soul longed to desire Your judgments.”

verses.text: And, “The desire of wisdom bringeth to a kingdom.”
verses.modernizedText: And, “The desire of wisdom brings to a kingdom.”

verses.text: Yet there has always obtained the usage of understanding desire and concupiscence in a bad sense if the object be not defined.
verses.modernizedText: Yet there has always obtained the usage of understanding desire and concupiscence in a bad sense if the object be not defined.

verses.text: But joy is used in a good sense: “Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, ye righteous.”
verses.modernizedText: But joy is used in a good sense: “Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, you righteous.”

verses.text: And, “Thou hast put gladness in my heart.”
verses.modernizedText: And, “You have put gladness in my heart.”

verses.text: And, “Thou wilt fill me with joy with Thy countenance.”
verses.modernizedText: And, “You will fill me with joy with Your countenance.”

verses.text: Fear is used in a good sense by the apostle when he says, “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling.”
verses.modernizedText: Fear is used in a good sense by the apostle when he says, “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling.”

verses.text: And, “Be not high-minded, but fear.”
verses.modernizedText: And, “Be not high-minded, but fear.”

verses.text: And, “I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.”
verses.modernizedText: And, “I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.”

verses.text: But with respect to sadness, which Cicero prefer to calls sickness (œgritudo), and Virgil pain (dolor) (as he says, “Dolent gaudentque”), but which I prefer to call sorrow, because sickness and pain are more commonly used to express bodily suffering,—with respect to this emotion, I say, the question whether it can be used in a good sense is more difficult.
